metadata.title: TMUA 2021 · Paper 1
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both locate a perpendicular bisector by equating squared distances to two fixed points and cancelling the squared coordinate terms. The original asks for the whole joining line of equal-radius circle intersections; the candidate asks where that same equidistance line meets an axis.
sharedKnowledge: Equidistance from two fixed points
Subtracting squared-distance equations

matches.rationale: Both form a squared centre-to-point distance from coordinate differences. The original compares distances to two given centres; the follow-up first extracts a centre from a circle equation and tests a distance condition. Extracting that centre is additional follow-up work, not a shared prerequisite.
sharedKnowledge: coordinate differences
squared centre-to-point distance

matches.rationale: Both expand or read a polynomial integrand and evaluate its antiderivative between two limits. The candidate practises this integration step before a parameter minimum, whereas the original finds its limits from turning points first.
sharedKnowledge: Termwise polynomial antiderivative
Upper-minus-lower endpoint evaluation

matches.rationale: The candidate directly practises integrating a sum of powers and subtracting the complete lower-limit value. That is the original integration stage; it does not practise finding the limits by differentiation.
sharedKnowledge: Power-rule integration
Signed subtraction of endpoint evaluations

matches.rationale: Both differentiate a polynomial and solve the resulting zero-gradient equation. The candidate isolates the first stage of the original, where stationary inputs must be found before they can be used as integration limits.
sharedKnowledge: Differentiate a polynomial
Solve the zero-gradient equation

matches.rationale: Both connect arithmetic and geometric progression terms, eliminate the arithmetic difference, and reject an inadmissible geometric ratio before using the sum to infinity. The numerical term conditions differ, so the student must rebuild the equations.
sharedKnowledge: Express AP and GP terms algebraically
Eliminate the common difference
Use the convergent ratio in an infinite sum

matches.rationale: Both use the AP and GP rules on related terms to form one parameter equation. The candidate reorders its terms and finishes with an AP sum, so it extends the same term-matching operation without reusing the original numerical conditions.
sharedKnowledge: Translate AP and GP term positions
Eliminate a parameter using both progression rules

matches.rationale: Both recover a convergent GP ratio from an arithmetic relation among selected terms, then use the geometric sum formula. The candidate uses a first-second-fourth term condition rather than sums of two progressions.
sharedKnowledge: Match nonconsecutive GP terms to an AP
Filter the ratio before summing

matches.rationale: Both replace a repeated exponential by a positive variable and complete a quadratic square. The candidate adds a positive reciprocal, so the student must use the denominator minimum to identify a maximum rather than simply report the quadratic minimum.
sharedKnowledge: Replace repeated exponential by a positive variable
Complete the square and check attainment

matches.rationale: Both expose a quadratic in a repeated exponential, complete its square and check the substituted range. The candidate has a bounded exponential-of-sine range, so its requested maximum must be found at an allowed endpoint.
sharedKnowledge: Quadratic in an exponential
Optimise on the attainable substituted interval

matches.rationale: The candidate practises the original first operation: combine the powers into a single exponential variable so that the remaining equation is quadratic. It solves for two inputs rather than minimising the quadratic, so it is a prerequisite transfer.
sharedKnowledge: Convert exponentials to a quadratic in one positive variable

matches.rationale: The original uses the cosine range to bound a simplified positive reciprocal. The candidate isolates the same range-propagation step through sine and cosine compositions, including whether each extreme is attained; it does not practise algebraic cancellation.
sharedKnowledge: Propagate the complete attainable trigonometric range
Check extrema under a monotone outer function

matches.rationale: Both use the Pythagorean identity to replace sine squares by an expression in cosine squares, or vice versa, before ordinary algebra. The candidate transforms a polynomial for the squared trigonometric values; the original uses the same conversion to factor a denominator.
sharedKnowledge: Use sine squared plus cosine squared equals one
Rewrite all trigonometric squares in one quantity

matches.rationale: Both name the unknown areas on sign-controlled intervals and translate given signed integrals into simultaneous linear equations. The candidate asks for total unsigned area, while the original then reflects the positive-input part of its graph.
sharedKnowledge: Separate positive lobe areas from signed integrals
Solve linear equations for unknown areas

matches.rationale: Both translate a transformed-function integral into an integral of the original function, then combine interval totals using the supplied equations. The original uses an input reflection and the candidate uses an input translation.
sharedKnowledge: Transform an integral interval
Combine signed interval totals

matches.rationale: Both interpret exactly one intersection with a line as a quadratic repeated-root condition. The candidate combines tangency with a known symmetry axis, whereas the original combines tangency to two different lines.
sharedKnowledge: A single line-parabola intersection is a repeated root
Use tangency to determine quadratic parameters

matches.rationale: The candidate practises reducing a two-equation intersection problem to a quadratic and interpreting its discriminant. It asks for two distinct intersections across a parameter range rather than the original repeated intersections.
sharedKnowledge: Eliminate one coordinate from two equations
Use the discriminant to count intersections

matches.rationale: Both choose a quadratic discriminant condition for a requested number of intersections. The candidate practises positive-discriminant two-root selection and parameter regions; the original needs zero-discriminant tangencies and simultaneous elimination.
sharedKnowledge: Both choose a quadratic discriminant condition for a requested number of intersections. The candidate practises positive-discriminant two-root selection and parameter regions; the original needs zero-discriminant tangencies and simultaneous elimination.

matches.rationale: Both require removing a modulus separately in regions where the input has a known sign. The candidate practises the sign-splitting step before integration; the original uses it to construct straight boundary segments in four quadrants.
sharedKnowledge: Replace absolute values using the sign of the input
Keep each replacement on its correct interval

matches.rationale: Both exploit axis symmetry of an absolute-value expression after solving one sign region, then use that symmetry to calculate a bounded area. The candidate has a curved one-variable boundary requiring integration rather than the original polygon triangles.
sharedKnowledge: Use absolute-value graph symmetry
Find one side of the boundary and reflect it for an area calculation

matches.rationale: The original must weight the logarithmic ordinates before combining them. The candidate isolates the same weighted-sum structure of the trapezium rule to track output transformations and error direction; it does not replace a fresh strip-width calculation.
sharedKnowledge: Trapezium estimates are weighted sums of ordinates
Carry output changes through the estimate

matches.rationale: Both end with a weighted algebraic expression in logarithms and must combine it into a single logarithm. The candidate practises that final logarithm-law step after exact polynomial integration, rather than the original numerical trapezium estimate.
sharedKnowledge: Simplify differences of logarithmic expressions
Combine the result into one logarithm

matches.rationale: Both rewrite fractional powers, differentiate and use a factored derivative sign chart to identify decreasing intervals. The candidate includes a zero-domain boundary, so that boundary must be separated from stationary roots.
sharedKnowledge: Differentiate fractional powers
Factor the derivative and determine its negative intervals

matches.rationale: Both use derivative factorisation and a sign chart to select intervals of monotonicity. The candidate compares two derivative signs, while the original measures the part of a fixed interval where one derivative is negative.
sharedKnowledge: Factor derivatives
Intersect increasing and decreasing sign intervals

matches.rationale: Both complete squares in two successive roles: first to express a minimum in terms of a parameter, then to use that parameter information in a second quadratic calculation. The candidate minimises across a family rather than using a prescribed first minimum.
sharedKnowledge: Complete a square to isolate a parameter-dependent minimum
Optimise the resulting quadratic expression

matches.rationale: The candidate practises completing a square in the parameter after another operation has produced a quadratic in it. This supports the original parameter-minimum reasoning, though the preceding operation is differentiation instead of a hidden squared-input substitution.
sharedKnowledge: Complete a square in a parameter
Distinguish minimising input from minimum output

matches.rationale: Both express a quadratic extremum as a function of a parameter and apply a stated numerical condition to it. The candidate uses a maximum below a bound instead of the original minimum equal to a given value.
sharedKnowledge: Express a quadratic extremum in terms of a parameter
Enforce a condition on that extremum

matches.rationale: Both start with the same type of unit-interval rule and require adding unit contributions to several longer integrals before summing those results. The candidate also reverses some bounds, so signs must be retained.
sharedKnowledge: Add unit-interval integral values
Build and sum several longer definite integrals

matches.rationale: The follow-up rehearses arithmetic-block summation used to build each cumulative integral in the original. The follow-up has linear integral terms forming an arithmetic progression; the original cumulative integral terms are triangular numbers, whose outer sum requires a further summation. This is a prerequisite transfer, not an identical sequence.
sharedKnowledge: sum a block of consecutive or linear values
connect an integral to a sequence term

matches.rationale: Both use the ranges of the two sides to restrict attention to a finite interval, then sketch a transformed cosine curve with a nontrigonometric curve and count distinct intersections. The candidate has a square-root curve instead of a parabola.
sharedKnowledge: Restrict the feasible input range
Count intersections of a trigonometric curve and a nontrigonometric curve

matches.rationale: Both count roots from intersections of two standard graphs without finding the roots explicitly. The candidate requires identifying the transformed tangent branches and checking excluded division cases; the original has a transformed cosine graph and a central contact.
sharedKnowledge: Use a transformed trigonometric graph
Count intersections branch by branch

matches.rationale: Both select specified binomial terms, retain all powers of the constant parameters and compare the resulting coefficient equations. The candidate equates coefficients across two expansions, while the original uses two coefficients from one expansion.
sharedKnowledge: Select complete binomial coefficients
Compare coefficient equations and divide nonzero factors

matches.rationale: Both recover unknown constants by matching selected coefficients in a binomial expansion. The candidate supplies end coefficients of a cube; the original supplies interior coefficients after identifying the degree.
sharedKnowledge: Use term positions to select powers
Match every constant factor in a binomial coefficient

matches.rationale: Both compare nonzero binomial coefficients so that division cancels common powers and exposes a relation between the parameters. The candidate then uses positive-integer restrictions; the original squares the resulting ratio.
sharedKnowledge: Take a ratio of nonzero binomial coefficient equations
Recover a relation between constant parameters

matches.rationale: The candidate practises finding the complete trigonometric solution set over a bounded interval. This is the first stage of the original before its allowed sine inputs are interpreted as squared circle radii; it does not practise the radius-spacing comparison.
sharedKnowledge: Solve a trigonometric equation on a specified interval
Filter impossible values and include valid endpoints

matches.rationale: The candidate isolates the conversion from a circle equation to its radius, including taking a square root. That is the original step that turns the allowed trigonometric inputs into radii; the candidate does not involve multiple concentric circles.
sharedKnowledge: Read a radius from a squared-coordinate equation

matches.rationale: The candidate practises moving a geometric centre through transformations and respecting the stated centre of an enlargement. This supports the original need to rotate displacement from the stated point, rather than rotate absolute coordinates; it is not another quarter-turn problem.
sharedKnowledge: Apply a transformation to a distinguished centre point
Distinguish a transformation centre from shape size

matches.rationale: Both use the vertex revealed by completing the square as a landmark for a transformed parabola. The candidate compares scaling and translation of that vertex, whereas the original rotates it about a separate point and then derives the transformed equation.
sharedKnowledge: Complete a quadratic square to locate its vertex
Track the vertex under a curve transformation

matches.rationale: Both restrict an intermediate trigonometric quantity to its attainable range, solve for its permitted values and then recover every original angle in the given interval. The candidate uses absolute cosine rather than a nested exponential inside sine.
sharedKnowledge: Solve for allowable trigonometric values
Recover and count distinct angles in the original interval

matches.rationale: Both recover all original angles after solving an equation in a trigonometric value and must include allowed interval endpoints. The candidate is particularly useful for the original zero-angle and upper-endpoint bookkeeping.
sharedKnowledge: Filter roots using the cosine range
Count endpoint solutions separately

matches.rationale: Both combine logarithms into algebraic equations and then check the original positive-argument restrictions rather than accepting the algebra alone. The candidate practises that equivalence-and-domain step without the original circle-arc geometry.
sharedKnowledge: Convert logarithmic equations to algebra
Retain every original logarithm domain

matches.rationale: The candidate rehearses converting an expanded two-variable quadratic into a circle equation and retaining its geometric validity condition. This is the original middle stage after logarithm elimination, before selecting the allowed arc.
sharedKnowledge: Complete both coordinate squares
Interpret the resulting centre and squared radius

matches.rationale: The candidate practises connecting an arc length with radius and a central angle in radians. This is the final geometric calculation required by the original once its logarithm domain has selected an arc; the candidate uses similar sectors instead of a domain-selected circle.
sharedKnowledge: Use the radius and central angle in an arc-length calculation
